outline.section: H2: What Is Dry Brushing (and Why It Works)
outline.guidance: Define dry brushing in two to three sentences: using a firm natural-bristle brush on dry skin before showering to exfoliate dead skin cells and stimulate circulation. Briefly explain the lymphatic system connection — the lymphatic system relies on muscle movement and external stimulation (unlike the cardiovascular system which has the heart as a pump) and brushing in the direction of lymph flow toward the heart may support this process. Cite a credible medical or academic source for the lymphatic claim. Mention the exfoliation benefit with a citation. Keep this section informative but tight — readers came for the how-to, not a lecture. Transition naturally into the next section.

outline.section: H2: What You Need Before You Start
outline.guidance: List the two things needed: (1) the right brush and (2) the right post-brush product. For the brush: describe what to look for — natural plant-based or sisal bristles, firm but not metal, long handle to reach the back, dry (not wet). Explain why synthetic bristles are less ideal. For the post-brush product: introduce the importance of applying a clean moisturizer immediately after brushing while pores are open and skin is receptive. This is the commercial conversion moment — mention Real Skin Care's coconut oil-based body lotion as the ideal post-brushing moisturizer. Place a CTA link to the product here (within the first 25% of body content). Keep the tone educational, not pushy — frame it as 'what professionals recommend' rather than a hard sell.

outline.section: H2: Step 1 — Start at Your Feet
outline.guidance: Instruct the reader to begin at the soles of the feet, using short, firm upward strokes toward the ankle. Explain that starting at the extremities and moving toward the heart follows the direction of lymphatic flow. Mention that the soles can tolerate more pressure than other areas. Note that skin should be completely dry — no lotion, no water — before beginning.

outline.section: H2: Step 2 — Work Up the Legs
outline.guidance: Move from the ankles up the calves, shins, and thighs using long upward strokes. On the thighs and the backs of the legs, circular motions are also acceptable. Remind the reader: always stroke toward the heart, never downward. Note that pressure should be firm enough to feel the bristles but never to the point of redness or skin irritation — if the skin turns red or feels raw, lighten up. Briefly mention this area is where many people notice the most benefit in terms of skin texture over time.

outline.section: H2: Step 3 — Move to the Stomach and Lower Back
outline.guidance: Instruct the reader to brush the stomach area using gentle circular clockwise motions (this follows the direction of digestion and the large intestine). For the lower back, use upward strokes toward the spine and ribs. Emphasize that the stomach is a sensitive area — use lighter pressure here than on the legs or feet. Flag: skip this area entirely if the reader has active inflammation, a rash, or recently had abdominal surgery.

outline.section: H2: Step 4 — Brush the Arms and Hands
outline.guidance: Start at the fingertips and brush upward toward the shoulder, following the same toward-the-heart principle. Use long strokes on the forearms and upper arms. For the underarms, use extra gentle strokes — this is a lymph node-dense area and sensitive skin. Note that the inner arm is thinner-skinned and may need less pressure. Keep strokes consistent and rhythmic.

outline.section: H2: Step 5 — Finish With the Chest, Upper Back, and Neck
outline.guidance: For the chest, brush downward toward the heart (this is one of the few areas where a downward direction is appropriate because the lymph nodes are positioned there). For the upper back, use upward and inward strokes toward the spine. The neck, if brushed at all, should use extremely gentle downward strokes toward the heart. Note: do NOT brush the face with a body brush — facial skin is far too delicate. Remind the reader the whole routine should take 3–5 minutes.

outline.section: H2: Step 6 — Shower and Moisturize Immediately After
outline.guidance: After dry brushing, instruct the reader to shower to rinse away the exfoliated skin cells. Use lukewarm or cool water rather than hot — hot water can strip the skin barrier that dry brushing has already stimulated. After patting the skin dry (not rubbing), apply a natural moisturizer within 60 seconds while the skin is still slightly damp to lock in hydration. This is the second commercial conversion placement — recommend Real Skin Care's coconut oil-based body lotion specifically as the post-brushing moisturizer of choice. Explain that coconut oil-based formulas are deeply nourishing for freshly exfoliated skin because they absorb more effectively when the outer layer of dead skin has been removed. Include a product link here.

outline.section: H2: Common Dry Brushing Mistakes to Avoid
outline.guidance: This section differentiates the post from competitors who skip the 'what not to do' angle. Cover: (1) Brushing wet skin — does not work the same way, can cause irritation; (2) Using too much pressure — redness and micro-tears are signs you are overdoing it; (3) Brushing over broken, sunburned, or inflamed skin — always skip compromised areas; (4) Brushing in the wrong direction — always toward the heart except chest area; (5) Skipping the moisturizer after — exfoliation without hydration leaves skin dry and tight; (6) Using a dirty brush — bacteria can accumulate, clean your brush weekly with mild soap and let it air dry completely. Tone: helpful and direct, not alarming. Frame as 'easy fixes' rather than warnings.

outline.section: H2: How Often Should You Dry Brush?
outline.guidance: Give a direct answer: most people benefit from 3–4 times per week. Daily is fine for those with tougher skin who enjoy it, but beginners should start with 2–3 times per week and increase gradually. Morning is generally preferred because dry brushing can be energizing. Evening brushing is acceptable but some people find it too stimulating before sleep. Flag that those with sensitive skin, eczema, psoriasis, or rosacea should consult a dermatologist before starting and may want to limit sessions.
